A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. tax_1833 stands against this person's name by 31 December 1833 and nothing says when they came. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Pryne, Peter” (tax_1833_086, line 138); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Pryne, Peter” (poll_1834_091, line 260); Poll list of 1835 — “Pryne, Peter” (poll_1835_060, line 347). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Pryne' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

merge_ruling.for_merge: Peter Pruyne is one of the better-documented men in the town — with Edmund Stoughton Kimberly he opened Chicago's second drug store early in 1833; he bought lot 1 of block 23 and lot 3 of block 119 of the school section on 24 and 25 October 1833 and town lots after; he married Rebecca Sherman on 20 August 1835; he polled in ward 1 at the first city election of 2 May 1837; Genealogy Trails' early-settler death notices print 'Pruyne, Peter, died November, 1839'. A man of that standing is one the town's own tax and poll rolls should carry, and the only entry of the stem on any of them is “Pryne, Peter” — tax_1833_086 (line 138), poll_1834_091 (line 260) and poll_1835_060 (line 347). The resident layer holds exactly one card of each spelling and no other bearer of the stem at all.
merge_ruling.against_merge: THE PAGE C9 ASKS FOR DOES NOT EXIST, and C9's demonstration is its load-bearing clause. No publication reached is caught setting both spellings. The IRAD rolls print Pryne three times and Pruyne never. The ISA land register prints 'PRUYNE P', 'PRUYNE P AND CO' and 'PRUYNE PETER' eighteen times and Pryne never. The whole deposited 1833-1835 newspaper run prints the stem 239 times, every one of them Pruyne. Moses & Kirkland print Pruyne and Pruyn; Fergus prints Pruyne. The two bodies of evidence never touch: the town's rolls know only Pryne, and the books, the press and the register know only Pruyne. Folding on what is left — one letter — is precisely what T-1001 measured and refused. AND THE TWO SPELLINGS APPEAR ON ONE SITE WITHOUT MEETING ON ONE PAGE: Genealogy Trails carries 'Pruyne, Peter' in earlysettlerobits and 'Pryne, Peter' in polllist, but those are its transcriptions of two different ORIGINALS, and a republisher's inconsistency across two documents is not a printer's inconsistency inside one, which is the thing C9 asks for.
